analysis.one_liner: Repeals the land swap that hands the Oak Flat federal area to foreign-owned copper miners.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 3, 2025 with 33 Democratic cosponsors, the bill sits in the House Natural Resources Committee with no hearing or vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2014, Congress tucked a provision into a defense bill requiring the Forest Service to hand Oak Flat — about 2,422 acres of federal land in Arizona sacred to Western Apache tribes — to Resolution Copper, a mining company owned by Rio Tinto and BHP. This bill would repeal that provision and permanently withdraw Oak Flat from mining and other disposal, keeping the land in public hands.
analysis.who_benefits: Western Apache tribes, for whom Oak Flat is a sacred ceremonial site listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and residents of the Phoenix area's East Salt River Valley, who rely on the same groundwater the mine would draw down. The bill's findings describe the mine consuming over 250 billion gallons of groundwater over 40 years and causing land subsidence that could cost Arizona billions in state trust land value.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Apache tribes and Phoenix-area water users

how_it_helps.text: Repeals section 3003 of Public Law 113-291, which requires the Forest Service to give Oak Flat to Resolution Copper within 60 days of a final environmental review.
Withdraws Oak Flat from all forms of mining entry, disposal, and mineral leasing, keeping the roughly 2,422 acres under public ownership subject to existing rights.

Preserves a site listed on the National Register of Historic Places as the Chi'chil Biᴉdagoteel Traditional Cultural Property, protecting it from the planned two-mile-wide, over-1,000-foot-deep crater the mine would create underground.

Protects regional groundwater: the bill's findings state the mine would consume over 250 billion gallons over 40 years and cause land subsidence, which the Arizona State Land Department objected to in an August 2025 letter to the Forest Service.

analysis.who_pays: Rio Tinto and BHP, through their Resolution Copper joint venture, would lose a congressionally mandated transfer of public land sitting atop one of the largest known copper deposits in the world. The copper does not disappear from public demand, but a major new domestic source would not open, and domestic copper supply would remain tighter than it otherwise would be.
analysis.who_pays_short: Rio Tinto and BHP's mining venture

drawbacks.text: The United States imports a significant share of its copper, which is central to electrification, grids, and batteries; blocking a large domestic copper mine leaves domestic supply tighter and could push demand toward imports, including from China — the very market the bill's findings criticize.

The bill offers no substitute site, compensation, or alternative project for Resolution Copper, which has spent roughly two decades and substantial capital on permitting and environmental review for this specific deposit.
The mining withdrawal is subject to 'valid rights in existence' at enactment, so any private claims already perfected at Oak Flat would survive the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and lasting: a sacred site preserved, a major water source in a drought-stricken region protected, and public land kept public. The cost is real but narrower: a forgone copper supply in a country that needs more of it, and a company's sunk investment. On balance, the trade favors the public, though Congress could reasonably pair protection of Oak Flat with a broader domestic minerals strategy rather than leaving copper policy unaddressed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on December 3, 2025 and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, where it awaits any hearing or action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 3, 2025 by Rep. Adelita Grijalva and referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
Thirty-three House Democrats have cosponsored the bill; no Republican has.

The underlying law this bill would repeal, section 3003 of Public Law 113-291, remains in effect and requires the Forest Service to convey Oak Flat to Resolution Copper once a final environmental impact statement is published.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: because the bill has not advanced, the 2014 land-transfer law remains in effect and Resolution Copper's project continues moving toward acquiring Oak Flat.

for.name: Rep. Adelita Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Oak Flat land transfer and withdraw the land from mining.

for.name: Western Apache tribes, led by the San Carlos Apache
for.role: Communities for whom Oak Flat is sacred land
for.what_they_did: Have campaigned for years to stop the transfer of Oak Flat to Resolution Copper.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 cosponsors are House Democrats and none are Republicans, and the Republican-majority House Natural Resources Committee has taken no action since the December 3 referral.

industries.industry: Foreign-owned copper mining (Rio Tinto and BHP's Resolution Copper)
industries.note: The bill repeals the 2014 law requiring the government to hand over Oak Flat, blocking the joint venture's access to one of the world's largest copper deposits. The mine would consume over 250 billion gallons of groundwater over 40 years and destroy a sacred site, so the companies' gain has come directly at the public's and the tribes' expense.

industries.industry: Arizona land development and Phoenix-area housing
industries.note: The Arizona State Land Department warned that mine-related groundwater pumping would cause subsidence and fissures on state trust land earmarked for residential development in the growing Phoenix metro area, jeopardizing billions in value that funds public education. Halting the pumping protects that land.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding a House majority and no Republican cosponsors, the bill is very likely to remain in committee without a hearing or floor vote for the rest of this Congress. Unless Congress acts, the 2014 land-transfer provision stays in effect and Resolution Copper can proceed toward acquiring Oak Flat when the environmental review process concludes.
